genres.Narrative: Narrative shows more than it tells. It reports what happened, including what people did wrong, without always pausing to say so. Ask what the storyteller is showing you through the events, not only what the characters say.
genres.Law: Law was given to a particular people inside a covenant at a particular time. Ask what it taught Israel about God and holiness before you ask how, or whether, it carries over to you.
genres.Poetry: Poetry speaks in image, parallelism, and feeling, not in flat prose. It tells the truth on a slant. Do not press a metaphor into a doctrine it was never built to carry.
genres.Wisdom: Wisdom gives the general shape of how life tends to go under God, not ironclad promises. A proverb is a wise observation about the way things usually run, not a guarantee.
genres.Prophecy: Prophecy mostly calls a people back to the covenant in their own day before it ever predicts the far future. Ask first what it meant to the people who first heard it.
genres.Gospel: A gospel is a theological portrait of Jesus, not a flat biography. Each writer selects and arranges to show you who Jesus is. Read each on its own terms before you harmonize them.
genres.Epistle: A letter was written to specific people about specific things. Read the whole argument, and watch for the therefore and the because that carry it, before you lift a single verse out of it.
genres.Apocalyptic: Apocalyptic writes in vision and symbol to a people under pressure, pulling back the curtain to show that God reigns over history. Expect images that point beyond themselves, not a coded calendar.

books.author: Traditionally Moses. Many scholars see older sources gathered and shaped over time.
books.audience: Israel, learning where it and the whole world came from.
books.occasion: To tell how God made everything good, how it broke, and how he began to mend it through one family.
books.date: Events reach back to the beginning. Written and compiled across the second and first millennia before Christ.
books.summary: Chapters one to eleven give the beginnings of the world and its fall. Chapters twelve to fifty follow Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph.

books.author: Traditionally Moses.
books.audience: Israel, a people just made free.
books.occasion: To tell how God rescued his people from Egypt and bound himself to them at Sinai.
books.date: The exodus is dated by some to the fifteenth and by others to the thirteenth century before Christ.
books.summary: Rescue out of slavery, the Passover, the Red Sea, the law at Sinai, and the tabernacle where God comes to dwell.

books.author: Traditionally Moses.
books.occasion: To teach a rescued people how a holy God can live in their midst.
books.date: Second or first millennium before Christ.
books.summary: Sacrifice, priesthood, clean and unclean, the Day of Atonement, and a call to be holy because God is holy.

books.author: Traditionally Moses.
books.occasion: To recount the forty years between Sinai and the edge of the promised land.
books.date: Second or first millennium before Christ.
books.summary: Two countings of the people frame a generation that doubts, rebels, and dies in the desert while God stays faithful.

books.author: Traditionally Moses, with the account of his death added.
books.audience: The new generation about to enter the land.
books.occasion: Moses preaches the law again before he dies, calling Israel to love and obey God.
books.date: Second or first millennium before Christ.
books.summary: Sermons that retell the journey, restate the covenant, and set life and death before the people as a choice.

books.author: Anonymous. Linked by tradition to Joshua and later editors.
books.occasion: To tell how God gave the promised land and to call the people to keep covenant in it.
books.date: Events around the late second millennium before Christ. Written later.
books.summary: Crossing the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the conquest, the dividing of the land, and a final charge to choose whom to serve.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.audience: Israel in the land before the kings.
books.occasion: To show the downward spiral of a people who keep forgetting God.
books.date: Written during the monarchy, looking back.
books.summary: A repeating cycle of sin, oppression, rescue by a judge, and relapse, ending in chaos because everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To tell a quiet story of loyalty and redemption in the days of the judges.
books.date: Written during or after the monarchy.
books.summary: A widowed foreigner clings to Israel and to Israel's God, and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To tell how Israel moved from judges to kings, for better and worse.
books.summary: Samuel, the rise and fall of Saul, and the anointing of David, the shepherd who will be king.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To tell the reign of David, his covenant, and his grievous fall.
books.summary: David's kingdom, God's promise of an everlasting throne, and the sin and sorrow that follow him to the end.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.audience: Israel and Judah, eventually in exile.
books.occasion: To explain how the kingdom rose, split, and started its long decline.
books.date: Reached its final form during or after the exile.
books.summary: Solomon's glory and the temple, the kingdom torn in two, and the prophets Elijah confronting the kings.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To account for why both kingdoms fell, naming covenant unfaithfulness as the cause.
books.date: Reached its final form during or after the exile.
books.summary: Elisha, the fall of the northern kingdom to Assyria, and the fall of Judah and Jerusalem to Babylon.

books.author: Anonymous. Traditionally linked to Ezra.
books.occasion: To retell Israel's story around the temple and the throne of David, giving a discouraged people their identity again.
books.date: After the exile, fifth or fourth century before Christ.
books.summary: Genealogies from Adam, then the reign of David framed around preparing worship for God.

books.author: Anonymous. Traditionally linked to Ezra.
books.occasion: To trace the kings of Judah through the lens of the temple and faithfulness.
books.summary: Solomon's temple, the kings of Judah, the fall of Jerusalem, and the decree that lets the people go home.

books.author: Traditionally Ezra in part.
books.occasion: To record the return from exile and the rebuilding of the temple and the people.
books.summary: Two waves return from Babylon, the temple is rebuilt, and Ezra calls the people back to the law.

books.author: Drawing on Nehemiah's own memoirs.
books.occasion: To record the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall and the renewal of the covenant.
books.summary: Nehemiah rebuilds the wall against opposition, and the people gather to hear the law and recommit.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To tell how God preserved his people from destruction in Persia, though his name is never spoken in the book.
books.date: Fifth or fourth century before Christ.
books.summary: A Jewish queen risks her life to save her people, and the festival of Purim is born.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.audience: Anyone who has suffered and asked why.
books.occasion: To wrestle with the suffering of a righteous person and the limits of human understanding.
books.date: Uncertain. Among the oldest material in the Bible.
books.summary: A blameless man loses everything, his friends explain it wrongly, and God answers not with reasons but with himself.

books.author: Many hands, including David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and others.
books.occasion: To give Israel words for every condition of the soul before God.
books.date: Composed across centuries, gathered after the exile.
books.summary: The prayer and praise book of the Bible. Lament, thanksgiving, trust, and kingship, set to be sung.

books.author: Mostly Solomon, with other named collectors.
books.audience: The young and the simple, learning to live well.
books.occasion: To teach the skill of living wisely in the fear of the Lord.
books.date: Composed and gathered across the monarchy and after.
books.summary: Short sayings on speech, money, work, friendship, and folly, all rooted in the fear of the Lord.

books.author: The Preacher, traditionally Solomon.
books.audience: Anyone tempted to think life under the sun is enough.
books.occasion: To face the vanity of life apart from God with unflinching honesty.
books.summary: A hard, clear-eyed search for meaning that ends by fearing God and keeping his commandments.

books.author: Traditionally Solomon.
books.occasion: To celebrate married love as a good gift, read by many also as a picture of God's love for his people.
books.summary: Love poems between a bride and her beloved, frank and tender.

books.author: Isaiah of Jerusalem. Many scholars see later prophets continuing in his name.
books.audience: Judah, facing Assyria and later exile.
books.occasion: To call a people to trust God rather than empires, and to promise a coming Servant who saves.
books.date: Eighth century before Christ and after.
books.summary: Judgment on pride, comfort for the exiles, and the suffering Servant who bears the sins of many.

books.author: Jeremiah, with his scribe Baruch.
books.audience: Judah, on the brink of and during exile.
books.occasion: To warn of judgment, weep over it, and promise a new covenant written on the heart.
books.date: Late seventh and early sixth century before Christ.
books.summary: The weeping prophet pleads with a people who will not turn, and points past the ruin to a new covenant.

books.author: Traditionally Jeremiah.
books.occasion: To grieve the destruction of the city while still hoping in God's mercy.
books.summary: Five poems of grief over a ruined Jerusalem, with mercies that are new every morning at their center.

books.author: Ezekiel, a priest in exile.
books.occasion: To explain the exile, promise return, and reveal the glory of God.
books.summary: Strange visions, the departing and returning glory of God, dry bones made to live, and a new temple.

books.author: Daniel. Date and authorship are debated.
books.audience: Faithful people living under hostile empires.
books.occasion: To show that God rules over kingdoms and will establish a kingdom that never ends.
books.date: Setting in the sixth century before Christ. Final form debated.
books.summary: Faithfulness in Babylon, the fiery furnace and the lions' den, and visions of empires and the Son of Man.

books.author: Hosea.
books.occasion: To picture God's faithful love for an unfaithful people through a prophet's painful marriage.
books.summary: God tells Hosea to love an unfaithful wife, a living parable of his love for wandering Israel.

books.author: Joel.
books.occasion: To call for repentance after a locust plague and to promise the outpouring of the Spirit.
books.summary: A locust plague becomes a warning of the day of the Lord, and a promise that the Spirit will be poured out on all.

books.author: Amos, a shepherd from Judah sent north.
books.occasion: To confront injustice and empty worship.
books.summary: A farmer turned prophet thunders against those who trample the poor while keeping the feasts.

books.author: Obadiah.
books.occasion: To pronounce judgment on Edom for gloating over Jerusalem's fall.
books.summary: The shortest Old Testament book. Pride brings Edom down, and the kingdom belongs to the Lord.

books.author: Anonymous.
books.occasion: To confront a people who would rather see enemies destroyed than saved.
books.summary: A prophet runs from God, is swallowed and spat out, preaches to Nineveh, and sulks when it repents.

books.author: Micah.
books.occasion: To indict injustice and false security, and to promise a ruler from Bethlehem.
books.summary: Judgment on corrupt leaders, the famous call to do justice and love mercy, and a coming shepherd-king.

books.author: Nahum.
books.occasion: To announce the fall of Nineveh.
books.summary: The God who is slow to anger will not leave the guilty unpunished, and cruel Nineveh will fall.

books.author: Habakkuk.
books.occasion: To wrestle honestly with why God uses a wicked nation to judge his own.
books.summary: A prophet argues with God about justice and learns that the righteous will live by faith.

books.author: Zephaniah.
books.occasion: To warn of the day of the Lord and call for humble seeking of God.
books.summary: A coming day of judgment that ends with God rejoicing over a humble remnant with singing.

books.author: Haggai.
books.occasion: To stir a discouraged people to rebuild the temple.
books.summary: Stop paneling your own houses and build the house of God, and the latter glory will be greater.

books.author: Zechariah.
books.occasion: To encourage temple rebuilding and point to the coming king.
books.summary: Night visions, the branch, and a humble king coming on a donkey, much of it taken up in the gospels.

books.author: Malachi.
books.occasion: To rebuke half-hearted worship and promise the coming messenger.
books.summary: The last Old Testament voice calls a tired people back, and promises Elijah before the great day.

books.author: Traditionally Matthew the tax collector.
books.occasion: To show that Jesus is the promised Messiah and king who fulfills the Old Testament.
books.summary: Jesus as the new Moses and son of David. Five great teaching blocks, including the Sermon on the Mount.

books.author: Traditionally Mark, drawing on Peter.
books.audience: Likely believers in Rome under pressure.
books.occasion: To present Jesus the suffering Son of God who calls disciples to follow him to the cross.
books.date: Roughly the late 50s to 60s after Christ.
books.summary: The shortest, fastest gospel. Jesus acts, the disciples are slow, and the road leads to Jerusalem and the cross.

books.author: Traditionally Luke the physician, companion of Paul.
books.audience: Theophilus and the wider non-Jewish world.
books.occasion: To give an orderly, researched account of Jesus, with special care for the poor and the outsider.
books.summary: Jesus the savior of all, full of prayer, mercy, and meals with sinners. Part one of a two-part work with Acts.

books.author: Traditionally John the apostle, the beloved disciple.
books.occasion: To lead readers to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.
books.summary: Seven signs and seven I am sayings reveal who Jesus is. The most reflective of the four gospels.

books.author: Luke.
books.occasion: To tell how the gospel went from Jerusalem to Rome by the power of the Spirit.
books.summary: Pentecost, the early church, and the missions of Peter and especially Paul to the ends of the earth.

books.author: Paul.
books.audience: The churches in Rome, whom Paul had not yet met.
books.occasion: To set out the gospel in full before visiting, uniting Jewish and non-Jewish believers around it.
books.summary: Paul's fullest statement of the gospel. Sin, justification by faith, the Spirit, Israel, and the life that follows.

books.author: Paul.
books.audience: The divided, gifted, immature church in Corinth.
books.occasion: To answer their questions and correct their divisions, immorality, and confusion about worship.
books.summary: Unity over division, the wisdom of the cross, freedom and love, the gifts, and the resurrection.

books.author: Paul.
books.occasion: To defend his ministry against rivals and to reconcile with a wounded church.
books.summary: Paul's most personal letter. Weakness, comfort, the new covenant, generosity, and power made perfect in weakness.

books.author: Paul.
books.audience: Churches in Galatia tempted to add law to the gospel.
books.occasion: To defend salvation by faith alone against those requiring works of the law.
books.date: Roughly the late 40s to mid 50s after Christ.
books.summary: No other gospel. Justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law, and free to walk by the Spirit.

books.author: Paul. Some scholars question this.
books.audience: The church in Ephesus and nearby.
books.occasion: To lift believers' eyes to God's great plan to unite all things in Christ.
books.summary: Chosen in Christ, saved by grace, made one new people, and called to live worthy of that calling.

books.author: Paul.
books.occasion: To thank them, encourage joy in suffering, and warn against pride and false teachers.
books.date: Roughly the early 60s after Christ, from prison.
books.summary: Joy from a prison cell, the great hymn of Christ's humbling and exaltation, and rejoicing always.

books.author: Paul. Some scholars question this.
books.occasion: To exalt the supremacy of Christ against a teaching that diminished him.
books.summary: Christ is supreme over all things and enough for everything, so do not add to him.

books.author: Paul.
books.occasion: To encourage new believers under pressure and answer their questions about the Lord's return.
books.date: Roughly 50 after Christ, one of Paul's earliest letters.
books.summary: Comfort for the grieving and the persecuted, and clear hope in the coming of the Lord.

books.author: Paul. Some scholars question this.
books.occasion: To correct confusion about the day of the Lord and to settle the idle.
books.summary: The Lord has not already come, so stand firm, keep working, and do not grow weary in doing good.

books.author: Paul. Authorship of the pastoral letters is debated.
books.audience: Timothy, leading the church at Ephesus.
books.occasion: To guide a young pastor in sound teaching, order, and leadership.
books.date: Roughly the early to mid 60s after Christ.
books.summary: How to conduct the household of God. Sound doctrine, prayer, leaders, and contentment over the love of money.

books.author: Paul. Authorship of the pastoral letters is debated.
books.occasion: Paul's last words from prison, charging Timothy to guard the gospel.
books.date: Roughly the mid to late 60s after Christ.
books.summary: Preach the word, endure hardship, and finish the race. Paul's farewell as death draws near.

books.author: Paul. Authorship of the pastoral letters is debated.
books.audience: Titus, organizing the church on Crete.
books.occasion: To set the churches in order and tie sound doctrine to good lives.
books.date: Roughly the early to mid 60s after Christ.
books.summary: Appoint faithful leaders, teach what is sound, and let grace train us to live upright lives.

books.author: Paul.
books.audience: Philemon, a believer and slave owner.
books.occasion: To ask Philemon to receive back his runaway slave Onesimus as a brother.
books.summary: A short, personal plea for forgiveness and reconciliation that quietly undermines slavery.

books.author: Anonymous. The author is unknown.
books.audience: Jewish believers tempted to drift back from Christ.
books.occasion: To show that Christ is greater than everything that came before and worth holding onto.
books.summary: Jesus is better than angels, Moses, and the old priesthood. The better covenant, so do not fall away.

books.author: Traditionally James, the brother of Jesus.
books.occasion: To call a faith that is real to show itself in how a person actually lives.
books.date: Possibly one of the earliest letters, or later.
books.summary: Faith without works is dead. Plain wisdom on the tongue, the poor, patience, and prayer.

books.author: Peter.
books.audience: Believers scattered and suffering across Asia Minor.
books.occasion: To strengthen Christians facing hostility for their faith.
books.date: Roughly the early to mid 60s after Christ.
books.summary: Living hope through suffering. You are a chosen people, so stand firm and follow the suffering Christ.

books.author: Peter. Some scholars question this.
books.occasion: To warn against false teachers and scoffers who deny the Lord's return.
books.summary: Grow in grace, beware false teachers, and remember that the Lord is patient, not slow, about his coming.

books.author: Traditionally John the apostle.
books.audience: Churches troubled by those who had left.
books.occasion: To give believers assurance and to test true faith by belief, love, and obedience.
books.summary: God is light and God is love. Walk in the light, love one another, and know that you have eternal life.

books.author: Traditionally John the apostle.
books.audience: A particular church, called the elect lady.
books.occasion: To urge love and warn against welcoming deceivers.
books.summary: Walk in truth and love, and do not give a platform to those who deny that Christ came in the flesh.

books.author: Traditionally John the apostle.
books.occasion: To commend hospitality to traveling teachers and rebuke a domineering leader.
books.summary: Support those who work for the truth, and do not imitate Diotrephes who loves to be first.

books.author: Traditionally Jude, the brother of James and of Jesus.
books.occasion: To urge believers to contend for the faith against those who twist grace into license.
books.summary: Contend for the faith. A sharp warning against false teachers, ending in a great doxology.

books.author: John.
books.audience: Seven churches in Asia Minor under pressure.
books.occasion: To unveil the risen Christ and assure a suffering church that he reigns and will win.
books.date: Roughly the 90s after Christ, with some arguing earlier.
books.summary: Visions of the throne, the Lamb, the dragon, and the final triumph of God in a new heaven and earth.
